Lunar Soil Plant Growth With The Aid Of Inoculant
2024 Plant The Moon Challenge
Team Members: Luke Calabrese (Sophomore) and Liam Flanagan (Sophomore)
Abstract
For the Fall 2024 Plant The Moon Challenge, we investigated the growth of Round Black Spanish
radishes in lunar regolith simulant amended with varying proportions of worm castings and peat moss.
The experiment tested three treatment levels (38%, 28.5%, and 19% soil amendments) plus a control
using pure simulant, with two replicates per treatment except for the control. All plants received an
inoculant (UltraBio by HardyGro) at twice the recommended concentration. Plants in the 38% amendment
group (Trial 1) showed the strongest growth, with heights reaching approximately 10-12 cm, while the
control plant failed to thrive beyond initial germination. The 28.5% and 19% amendment groups showed
intermediate success, though one 28.5% sample failed to germinate. Unexpectedly, all surviving plants
demonstrated some growth despite the challenging substrate, suggesting the inoculant played a crucial
role in plant survival. Post-experiment soil analysis revealed distinct layering of components, potentially
affecting nutrient availability. Our findings suggest that while higher proportions of organic amendments
improve radish growth in lunar simulant, the bacterial inoculant may be crucial for even minimal plant
survival in lunar regolith conditions.
Team Roles
The size of the team prevented defined roles from taking shape. Both team members did
everything throughout the experiment. However, some things were more often handled by one member
than the other. Liam Flanagan almost always handled watering, and Luke Calabrese took height data, for
example.
Background
This experiment was conducted as part of the Fall 2024 Plant the Moon Challenge, a scientific
competition where teams from high schools across the USA competed to create the best substance to be
added to lunar simulant soil to facilitate plant growth. When we were presented with the challenge, our
teacher gave us a SchoolAI advisor who instructed us to give pertinent information. We utilized it to
decide what our approach to the challenge would be, such as types of plants to consider and substances
to add to the regolith to improve the health of the plants.
Plant Selection
Our first plan was to utilize potatoes, as they have a large amount of natural aluminum resistance
and work well with many kinds of helpful bacteria. However, potatoes take a space of about 20 cm² to
grow properly, and our space per plant was limited to about 9 cm². Furthermore, potatoes take 80 to 100
days to grow, and our growth period was limited to 8 weeks.
Therefore, we changed our plan to utilize radishes. Radishes also benefit from many kinds of
helpful bacteria, but they only take about 30 to 40 days to grow and thrive in the small space we had.
When it came to choosing our species, we had the privilege of communicating with Jessica Atkin, a NASA
intern who performed a similar experiment earlier in 2024 with chickpeas. While our first instinct was to

choose a radish species that grew quickly and required few nutrients, Ms. Atkin suggested that we
choose a species with high metal resistance, particularly aluminum, due to the high volume of metals in
lunar soil. Taking this advice, we found a species with a very interesting trait. According to our research,
the Round Black Spanish radish shows a slight increase in growth speed in high aluminum environments
(Kurina).
Soil Considerations
When deciding on what substances should comprise our additive, we first examined the major
concerns with growing plants in lunar regolith and came up with methods of addressing them. The first
major concern was the lack of nutrients in the soil. Our solution was vermicompost, a highly nutritious
substance, which made up the majority of our additives. The second major concern was pH. Plants grow
best in acidic environments, but the lunar regolith is slightly basic. Our solution to this problem was peat
moss, a plant substance that lowers the pH of the soil as it decomposes. The final major obstacle was the
drainage of the lunar soil. The lunar regolith has no substances in it to give it water retention, causing
water to drain to the bottom of the pot, where the plant's roots can't reach it. We first planned to include
water retention beads in the soil. However, when we consulted with Ms. Atkins, she informed us that peat
moss is an excellent retainer of water, and reminded us that radishes prefer sandy soils anyway, so we
scrapped the inclusion of water retention beads.
Growth Enhancement
The final component of the plan was the inoculant, which is helpful bacteria added to the soil to
promote plant growth. For this, we utilized a product called UltraBio by HardyGro, an additive to water
that contains many useful nutrients, bacteria, and fungi. We added the substance to our water at twice the
recommended amount, as suggested by Ms. Atkins.

Problem Definition
The core problem that underpins the experiment is that plants have difficulty growing on the moon
due to the gravity, sunlight, soil, and atmosphere. This experiment, however, focused on the soil concern.
There were many time and resource constraints placed upon us, such as an eight week growth period
and growth space of only about 0.5 liters per plant. Additionally, there were 5 other groups performing
their own experiments utilizing the same area, so the plants grown in this experiment were not centered
under the light. Furthermore, due to the nature of the experiment being conducted at school, the watering
schedule was occasionally off base due to the lack of the necessary class. The requirements were loose,
but our personal goal was for at least one of the plants to survive and grow healthy over the growth
period, proving the effectiveness of their method. Overall, the experiment was more a test of the inoculant
than the soil additive, giving it a unique position among the similar experiments conducted as part of the
challenge, which is more focused on the soil. They Were Planted on October 10, 2024.
Experimental Design
Hypothesis: Plants grown in lunar simulant soil with higher proportions of organic additives will
demonstrate better growth and health outcomes compared to those with lower proportions of additives.
Safety Protocols: Due to hazardous materials used in this experiment, the following safety measures
were used:
●
Masks and goggles when handling lunar simulant to prevent respiratory issues and eye irritation

●
Protective gloves when working with the inoculant due to potentially pathogenic bacteria
●
All soil mixing and planting was done in a well-ventilated area
●
Standard laboratory safety equipment (goggles, gloves) Utilized while planting
Growth Success Metrics:
●
Primary Metrics:
○
Plant height: continued growth
○
Survival rate through entire growth period
○
Successful germination within 5-7 days
●
Health Indicators:
○
Stem strength (ability to stand upright)
○
Root development at experiment conclusion
Variables:
●
Independent Variable: Proportion of soil additives in lunar simulant (38%, 28.5%, 19%, 0%)
●
Dependent Variables:
○
Plant height
○
Soil moisture content
●
Control Variables:
○
Light exposure (12-hour cycles)
○
Water volume (20 mL per plant)
○
Watering schedule (Monday/Thursday)
○
Inoculant concentration
○
Temperature
○
Growth period duration
Treatment Groups:
1. High Amendment (Trial 1): 38% additive
○
120 mL worm castings
○
32 mL peat moss
○
Two replicates
2. Medium Amendment (Trial 2): 28.5% additive
○
90 mL worm castings
○
24 mL peat moss
○
Two replicates

○
60 mL worm castings
○
16 mL peat moss
○
Two replicates
4. Control: 0% additive
○
Pure lunar simulant
○
One replicate

Sampling and Measurement Plan:
●
Measurements taken as often as possible
●
Watered twice a week (tuesday and friday)
●
Heights measured from soil surface to tallest point
●
Soil moisture readings taken before watering
●
Photo documentation when measured

Week 1:
●
Day 1: Planting
●
Days 5-7: Expected germination
Week 2:
●
Plant thinning at end of week
●
Begin regular height measurements
Weeks 3-7:
●
Continue regular measurements

●
Final measurements
●
Root system examination
●
Soil composition analysis
Expected Outcomes:
●
Control plant not expected to survive beyond germination
●
Low amendment plants are predicted to show minimal growth
●
Higher amendment groups are expected to show proportionally better growth
Results and Analysis
Growth Metrics
Initial Germination Results:
●
Germination occurred within the expected 5-7 day window for all treatments except one Trial 2
(28.5% additive) sample which failed to germinate
●
Control plant and trial 3-2 successfully germinated but survived only briefly
●
All other plants germinated successfully

Plant Heights:
Raw Data
●
Trial 1 (38% additive) showed the strongest growth, reaching 10-12 cm at the experiment
conclusion
●
Trial 2 (28.5% additive) achieved intermediate heights of 7-9 cm
●
Trial 3 (19% additive) showed variable results:
○
Trial 3-1 maintained growth
○
Trial 3-2 performed as expected with minimal growth before dying
●
Control plant survived only through the initial growth phase
Plant Health Assessment
Leaf Development:
●
Surviving plants developed true leaves beyond cotyledons
●
Plant slanting occurred consistently across treatments due to light seeking behavior
●
Height measurements were affected by plant slanting, requiring final measurements with manual
straightening
Soil Composition Effects:

●
Post-experiment soil analysis revealed distinct layering:
○
Bottom layer: Worm castings
○
Middle layer: Peat moss
○
Top layer: Lunar simulant
●
This layering may have affected nutrient distribution and root development
Soil Moisture Analysis
Raw Data
Moisture Patterns:
●
Soil moisture levels fluctuated between 10-75% across all treatments
●
Large spikes in readings (reaching 75%) likely due to either hardware malfunction or user error
●
No clear correlation between soil moisture levels and plant health or growth
●
All treatments showed similar moisture retention patterns despite different amendment ratios

Key Findings:
Treatment Effectiveness:
●
Higher amendment percentages (38%) consistently produced better growth outcomes
●
Inoculants appeared crucial for plant survival, even enabling brief control plant survival
●
Physical positioning relative to light source significantly impacted plant performance
●
Soil component separation may have influenced nutrient availability
Experimental Limitations:
●
Height measurements were complicated by plant slanting behavior
●
Soil moisture sensor readings showed unexplained variations
●
Light position variations created uncontrolled variables
●
Regular access limitations affected measurement consistency

Discussion
Hypothesis Evaluation
Our hypothesis that higher proportions of soil amendments would lead to better plant growth was
largely supported by the experimental results. Plants in Trial 1 (38% amendments) showed the strongest
growth and survival rates as predicted. However, we observed some unexpected deviations, particularly
the failure of one Trial 2 sample to germinate despite its moderate amendment level, and the surprising
initial success of the control plant which we had predicted would not germinate at all.
Key Findings and Interpretations
Soil Amendment Effects
The 38% amendment group demonstrated superior growth, suggesting this ratio may approach
optimal conditions for radish growth in lunar simulant. Post-experiment soil analysis revealed distinct
layering of components (worm castings, peat moss, lunar simulant), indicating either soil settling during
growth or insufficient initial mixing. The layering effect may have created nutrient gradients affecting root
development and nutrient access. Plant success generally correlated with amendment percentage,
supporting the value of organic additions to lunar regolith.
Inoculant Impact
The survival of all plants, including brief control plant growth, suggests the inoculant played a
crucial role in plant viability. The UltraBio bacterial supplement may have enhanced nutrient availability
even in low-amendment conditions. The double-strength inoculant application likely contributed to
better-than-expected survival rates. Results suggest biological amendments might be as important as
physical soil amendments.
Environmental Factors
Plant positioning relative to light source significantly affected growth patterns. Trial 1-1's higher
success despite suboptimal light positioning suggests other factors may have compensated.
Light-seeking behavior caused plant slanting, complicating height measurements. Shared growing space
with other experiments created unavoidable variations in light exposure.
Experimental Limitations
Technical Constraints
Limited growing space (0.5 liters per plant) may have restricted root development. Shared light
source created uneven growth conditions. Soil moisture sensor readings showed unexplained spikes,
suggesting potential measurement issues. The eight-week growth period prevented observation of full
plant maturity.
Procedural Challenges
School schedule affected consistent maintenance and observation. Soil component separation

indicated potential mixing methodology issues. Plant slanting required modified measurement techniques.
Regular access limitations impacted measurement consistency.
Future Research Directions
Direct comparison of inoculated versus non-inoculated samples would help isolate bacterial
effects. Alternative soil mixing methods should be investigated to prevent component separation. Testing
different plant species under similar conditions could yield valuable comparative data. Extended growth
periods would allow observation of full plant development. Examination of root development patterns in
layered soil conditions could provide insights into nutrient uptake mechanisms.
Broader Implications
While this experiment focused on lunar agriculture conditions, several key findings have broader
applications. The critical role of bacterial inoculants in challenging growth conditions highlights the
importance of microbial communities in agriculture. The separation of soil components demonstrates the
need for careful consideration of soil structure in amended growing media. The success of Round Black
Spanish radishes suggests their potential for growth in mineral-rich environments. Overall, these results
contribute to the growing body of knowledge about lunar agriculture while highlighting the importance of
both physical and biological soil amendments in extreme growing conditions.
